The Hawaiian grouper Hyporthodus quernus attains a maximum recorded total length of 122 centimeters [Li = 122 centimeters], making it one of the larger epinephelid species endemic to the Hawaiian Archipelago. Field surveys conducted around the main Hawaiian Islands indicate that females typically reach puberty at a total length of 58 centimeters [Lp = 58 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal development and the ability to contribute to spawning aggregations. The transition from juvenile to reproductive life stages appears closely tied to body size rather than chronological age, a pattern commonly observed among serranids. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis suggest that individuals invest heavily in somatic expansion before allocating resources to gamete production, a strategy that likely enhances reproductive success by allowing females to achieve a larger body size and thus greater fecundity at first spawning.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been measured at 1.5% [GSI = 1.5%] in gravid females during the peak spawning season when water temperatures hovered near 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. Such an iteroparous strategy could buffer against interannual variability in oceanographic conditions that affect larval survival. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from individuals collected at this thermal regime confirmed the presence of hydrated oocytes and post-ovulatory follicles, indicating active and recent spawning activity consistent with the measured GSI.

Eggs of the Hawaiian grouper are pelagic and possess a mean diameter of 0.533 millimeters, from which the wet weight at birth is calculated to be approximately 0.000079 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000079 grams], a minute mass typical of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, buoyant propagules. The tiny size of the fertilised ovum at the moment of chorion rupture reflects a life-history strategy centered on high fecundity and broad dispersal of offspring across the oceanic environment. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves for its initial days of development, with the duration of this lecithotrophic phase influenced markedly by ambient temperature. Enclosed within the protective chorion, the cleavage-stage embryo progresses rapidly through the blastula and gastrula stages before hatching enzyme secretion triggers emergence as a free-swimming prolarva.

From field-based length-weight relationships, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to the maximum recorded length of 122 centimeters is estimated at 33300 grams [Wwi = 33300 grams], representing the asymptotic mass that adults can achieve under favorable conditions. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty for females, derived from the 58-centimeter length threshold, is calculated to be 3500 grams [Wwp = 3500 grams], meaning that a female must more than quadruple her body mass between the onset of maturity and her potential maximum size. This substantial post-maturity growth permits a prolonged reproductive lifespan, allowing individuals to increase fecundity incrementally with each successive spawning season. The discrepancy between weight at maturity and ultimate weight underscores the selective advantage of delayed reproduction in favor of continued somatic investment, a pattern that makes the species particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure targeting larger, more fecund individuals.

The maximum lifespan of the Hawaiian grouper, based on mark-recapture studies and otolith aging from specimens collected across the archipelago, is estimated at 35 years [am = 35 years] for individuals inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. This extended longevity, among the greatest recorded for any epinephelid, is consistent with a life-history syndrome characterized by slow growth, late maturity, and high adult survival. The relatively cool waters of the Hawaiian Ridge, compared to tropical grouper habitats elsewhere, likely contribute to reduced metabolic rates and consequently slower senescence. However, such extreme longevity also renders the species acutely sensitive to overexploitation, as the removal of old, reproductively valuable individuals can take decades to replace through natural recruitment.
